Updated at 123 AM EDT Mon Sep 21 2026

- Well above normal temperatures to persist through Tuesday. But relief
  is on the way, with a pattern change expected mid-week and much
  cooler temperatures to follow.

sections.title: DISCUSSION
sections.text:
Issued at 123 AM EDT Mon Sep 21 2026

A weak shortwave will move into the Ohio valley during the day 
Monday and then push east of the forecast area by Tuesday morning, 
all of which is ahead of a closed upper low shifting east through 
the northern plains and into the Upper Midwest. At the surface, this 
wave will push a weak cold front towards the Tennessee valley during 
the day, lingering just to our west and northwest Monday night 
through Tuesday. As such, expect this to be a focus for increased 
convective coverage both Monday and Tuesday. Forecast soundings show 
enough instability to be concerned about a few strong to severe 
storms on Monday capable of damaging winds. The overall threat isn't 
high, but the combination of decent instability along with high 
PWATs means that a few damaging wind gusts similar to what was seen 
a day or two ago could occur. Additionally, with slow storm motions, 
some isolated flash flooding could occur. Tuesday will be similar in 
coverage as the Ohio valley upper low begins to shift southeast, but 
instability will be notably less so outside of the far southern 
parts of the area, think that any severe threat is low.

Regardless of the expected storms for Monday and Tuesday, the heat 
will continue. Highs in the 80s and 90s are expected.

On Wednesday the pattern change gets underway and we begin to see a 
break in the relentless heat. By Wednesday a rex block pattern takes 
shape as an upper ridge builds over the Canadian side of the Great 
Lakes region, and the aforementioned Ohio valley upper low deepens 
over the Ohio valley and central Appalachian region. With the upper 
low to our north and NW flow aloft, this will push the cold front 
through the southern Appalachians and allow the cooldown to begin. 
By Thursday through the weekend we should see highs topping out only 
in the 70's for every except southeast TN where they may squeak 
across the 80 degree mark. This pattern will also be fairly dry with 
a more Canadian airmass moving in.

sections.title: AVIATION
sections.text:
(06Z TAFS)
Issued at 123 AM EDT Mon Sep 21 2026

Main concern for the 06Z cycle will be the fog potential again and
how much, if any forms. The set up at TRI is similar to the
previous few nights so we have maintained IFR fog for a few hours.
Guidance remains more hesitant than previous nights so we kept 
VSBY a touch higher (1SM) than previous nights. It's possible 
I'll need to circle back and AMD in lower VSBY once it begins to 
develop.

A few isolated thunderstorms have developed over middle TN this
evening. They should stay clear of TYS and TRI, but we will need
to keep an eye on CHA as they could briefly impact them overnight.
Left out anything for now as it's generally low confidence. Attention
turns to afternoon thunderstorms later today. Storms are expected
to develop along approaching cold front moving through the 
region. Coverage is expected to be scattered. The better upper 
support for storms will be in the north so PROB30 groups at KTYS 
and KTRI for SHRA in the afternoon/evening period.

enso.title: ENSO Alert System Status: El Niño Advisory
paragraphs: ENSO Alert System Status: El Niño Advisory Synopsis: El Niño is strengthening, with a greater than 90% chance of a very strong event during the Northern Hemisphere fall and winter 2026-27. El Niño strengthened further over the past month, with sea surface temperature anomalies exceeding +3.0°C in the eastern equatorial Pacific [Fig. 1] . Except for the Niño-4 index, which decreased to +0.1°C in August, values in the other Niño indices increased, reaching +1.8°C in Niño-3.4, +2.5°C in Niño-3, and +3.4°C in Niño-1+2 [Fig. 2] . The equatorial subsurface temperature index (average from 180°-100°W) remained steady during August [Fig. 3] , reflecting a deeper-than-average thermocline [Fig. 4] . Subsurface temperatures continued to be significantly above average, with widespread anomalies in excess of +10.0°C at depth. Low-level westerly wind anomalies and upper-level easterly wind anomalies extended from the western to the east-central equatorial Pacific. Enhanced convection and rainfall persisted from the central to the eastern Pacific, while anomalies remained suppressed over Indonesia [Fig. 5] . The traditional and equatorial Southern Oscillation indices remained negative. Collectively, the coupled ocean-atmosphere system reflected a strengthening El Niño. The CPC Official ENSO outlook , which synthesizes multiple models from North America and abroad, indicates El Niño will continue to strengthen through the end of the year [Figs. 6

-8] . During the October-December 2026 season, there is a 75% chance of a historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950 (+2.5°C or more for a 3-month RONI value ). With an event of this magnitude, the chances of experiencing impacts consistent with El Niño are larger, though not guaranteed (see CPC outlooks for probabilities of seasonal anomalies). In summary, El Niño is strengthening, with a greater than 90% chance of a very strong event during the Northern Hemisphere fall and winter 2026-27. This discussion is a consolidated effort of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), NOAA's National Weather Service, and their funded institutions. Oceanic and atmospheric conditions are updated weekly on the Climate Prediction Center web site (

md.summary: The threat for severe weather is diminishing and the remaining valid portions of the watch may be cancelled prior to the 09Z expiration.
md.discussion: Recent trends in volumetric radar data indicate decreasing echo tops and updraft intensities owing to the presence of considerable convective inhibition and the resultant disruption of previous supercell structures. Ongoing storms over portions of Otero, Bent, and Prowers Counties in southeast CO may remain capable of locally gusty winds and sub-severe hail for the next hour or so. However, in general, the threat for organized severe weather appears to have ended.
